The strong devour the weak like fish in a pond. Fearing a collapse where even truth and security falter, the assembly urges Vasiṣṭha to consecrate a new ruler from the Ikṣvāku line.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे द्विषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Vasiṣṭha sends messengers to fetch Bharata.
chapters.es: Vasiṣṭha instructs messengers to travel to Rājagṛha. He commands them to fetch Bharata immediately while concealing the news of Daśaratha’s death and Rāma’s exile. Carrying silks and ornaments, the envoys cross the Gaṅgā at Hastināpura and ride through Kurujāṅgala and Pañcāla. They ford the Saradaṇḍā and Vipāśā rivers. Their journey concludes as they reach the gates of Girivraja at night to secure the continuity of the royal line.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे त्रिषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata describes a frightening dream about his father.
chapters.es: Messengers reach the city as Bharata wakes from a dream. His companions play music and perform plays, yet he does not smile. He describes seeing his father fall from a mountain peak into a pool of gomaya. In this vision, the king drinks taila, eats tilodana, and sits on an iron throne. Clad in black and wearing red garlands, the monarch drives a chariot pulled by asses toward the south. Bharata interprets these as signs of impending death.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे चतुःषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata travels home to Ayodhyā.
chapters.es: Messengers from Ayodhyā reach Rājagṛha to recall Bharata. Bharata inquires after the welfare of Daśaratha, Rāma, and his mothers, noting Kaikeyī’s temperament. The King of Kekaya grants him leave and bestows gifts of gold and specialized breeds of dogs. Accompanied by Śatrughna and a retinue of trusted ministers, Bharata mounts his chariot and leaves his grandfather’s palace. He leads a large convoy of horses and camels on the return journey.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे पञ्चषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata returns to Ayodhyā and finds it quiet.
chapters.es: Bharata crosses the Śatadrū and Yamunā rivers on mountain horses, passing through forests and crossing the Gomatī. After seven nights, he reaches the white-soiled city of Ayodhyā. He finds the streets silent and the gardens deserted. No music or voices of playing citizens sound from the walls. Residents appear tearful, and the city gates remain dusty. Sensing trouble, he enters through the Vaijayanta gate and walks toward his father's palace.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे षट्षष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Kaikeyī tells Bharata of the king's death.
chapters.es: Bharata enters Kaikeyī’s apartments, finding the palace joyless. Kaikeyī informs him that King Daśaratha has died. Stricken by grief, Bharata collapses and asks for his elder brother’s whereabouts. Kaikeyī reveals that she secured the kingdom for Bharata and forced Rāma into exile in the Daṇḍaka forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. She explains that the king died from the sorrow of separation. Kaikeyī then urges her son to assume the throne.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे सप्तषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata rebukes Kaikeyī and rejects the throne.
chapters.es: Bharata confronts Kaikeyī after learning of Daśaratha’s death and Rāma’s exile. He compares his mother to a fatal night that destroyed the royal lineage. Describing Rāma in garments of bark (cīra-valkala), Bharata rejects the kingdom, likening his inability to rule to a young bull collapsing under a heavy yoke. He vows to thwart her ambition by bringing his brother back from the forest. Finally, he bellows in grief like a lion inside a mountain cave.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे अष्टषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata rebukes Kaikeyī and vows to return Rāma.
chapters.es: Bharata condemns Kaikeyī for causing the king's death and Rāma’s exile. He calls her a destroyer of the lineage and predicts her descent into hell. To illustrate Kauśalyā’s suffering, he recounts how the divine cow Surabhi wept for her laboring sons until her tears fell upon Indra. Bharata vows to bring his brother back or enter the forest himself. He then collapses to the earth, his ornaments scattered like a fallen banner.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकोनसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata swears his innocence to Kauśalyā.
chapters.es: Bharata enters Kauśalyā’s residence and finds her trembling in soiled garments. Kauśalyā accuses him of accepting a kingdom won through Kaikeyī’s cruelty. To prove his innocence, Bharata utters several śapatha, or solemn oaths. He invokes the sins of those who kick a sleeping cow or fail to reward their servants. Convinced of his devotion to Rāghava, Kauśalyā embraces him as he falls to the ground in grief. They spend the night mourning together.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे सप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata performs the funeral rites for Daśaratha.
chapters.es: Vasiṣṭha directs Bharata to perform funeral rites for Daśaratha. Attendants remove the king’s body from its oil preservation and place it upon a jeweled couch. Bharata laments his father’s death and Rāma’s exile as a procession carries the litter toward the Sarayū. Priests construct a pyre of sandalwood and agaru, chanting Sāma hymns. The queens circumambulate the flames, wailing like krauñca birds. After offering water libations, the family returns to the city.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata performs funeral rites and mourns.
chapters.es: Bharata completes the ten-day mourning and performs śrāddha rites on the twelfth day, distributing wealth to brāhmaṇas. On the thirteenth day, he visits the cremation ground. The sight of the ashes causes both Bharata and Śatrughna to collapse. Vasiṣṭha and Sumantra intervene, reminding the princes of the inevitable dualities of life and death. The brothers rise like weathered banners of Indra, wiping their tears to finish the final purificatory rituals.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे द्विसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śatrughna attacks Mantharā and Bharata intervenes.
chapters.es: Śatrughna condemns the exile of Rāma and his father’s death. When Mantharā appears in royal garments, he seizes her and drags her through the palace. Her broken ornaments litter the floor like stars in an autumnal sky. He harshly rebukes Kaikeyī, who flees for protection. Bharata restrains his brother, arguing that Rāma would never approve of killing a woman. Yielding to this duty, Śatrughna releases the servant, whom Kaikeyī then comforts like a trapped bird.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे त्रिसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata refuses the crown to find Rāma.
chapters.es: At dawn on the fourteenth day, ministers and guilds urge Bharata to accept the kingship. Bharata circumambulates the ābhiṣecanika vessels but rejects the throne, insisting the eldest brother must rule. He vows to live in the forest for fourteen years and orders an army to prepare for Rāma’s return. He commands artisans to level the ground and clear a path to the wilderness. Hearing his devotion, the assembly begins the necessary preparations for the journey.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे चतुःसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Workers build a road for Bharata's journey.
chapters.es: Surveyors and laborers depart to prepare the way. They clear thickets, level uneven ground, and bridge gaps with soil and stone. These men dig wide reservoirs and line the path with flowering trees and banners. To facilitate Bharata’s progress, they build camps near fruit groves according to auspicious timings. Sprinkled with sandalwood water and strewn with petals, the finished mārga stretches toward the Gaṅgā, resembling a star-filled sky.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे पञ्चसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Vasiṣṭha summons a council and Bharata enters.
chapters.es: Bards wake Bharata with the rhythmic beat of dundubhi drums. This music only deepens his grief, leading him to reject the throne and lament Daśaratha’s death to Śatrughna. The sage Vasiṣṭha enters the hall and summons the ministers for an urgent council. As the leaders arrive on horses and elephants, the crowded assembly greets Bharata with the reverence once shown to his father, filling the hall like a tranquil lake.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे षट्सप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata refuses the crown to retrieve Rāma.
chapters.es: Bharata enters the assembly where Vasiṣṭha urges him to accept the vacant throne. Rejecting the crown, Bharata declares Rāma—the equal of kings like Dilīpa—the sole heir of the Ikṣvāku dynasty. He denounces his mother’s actions and vows to bring his brother back from the forest. At his command, Sumantra mobilizes the army. Soldiers and citizens harness horses and elephants to their chariots, preparing an expedition to restore the exiled prince.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे सप्तसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata leads his army to the Gaṅgā river.
chapters.es: Bharata departs in a chariot, followed by nine thousand elephants and sixty thousand archers. The queen mothers join the procession while citizens and artisans discuss Rāma’s complexion. Vedic brāhmaṇas follow the assembly in goratha carts. Upon reaching the Gaṅgā, Bharata instructs his ministers to halt the army. He prepares to offer water libations for his father and spends the night on the riverbank, contemplating how to persuade Rāma to return.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे अष्टसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Guha meets Bharata at the river bank.
chapters.es: Guha, the king of the Niṣādas, observes Bharata’s vast army encamped by the Gaṅgā. Fearing an attack on Rāma, he commands his kinsmen to arm five hundred boats and guard the riverbanks. He approaches the camp with offerings of fish, meat, and honey to discern Bharata’s intentions. Introduced by Sumantra, Guha offers local knowledge and forest produce as hospitality. He invites the prince and his troops to rest by the water.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकोनाशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata assures Guha of his loyalty.
chapters.es: Bharata asks Guha for the path to the hermitage of Bharadvāja. Guha offers archers as guides but questions the large army, fearing for Rāma. Bharata vows he only seeks to return his brother to the throne, earning the chief's praise. As night falls, Bharata encamps his men but remains awake, consumed by grief. His distress forms a duḥkhaśaila, a mountain of sorrow. Guha consoles the mourning prince as he sighs like the snows of the Himavat.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे अशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Guha tells Bharata about Lakṣmaṇa’s vigilance.
chapters.es: Guha tells Bharata how Lakṣmaṇa stood watch while Rāma and Sītā slept on grass. Refusing rest, Lakṣmaṇa spoke of his fears for King Daśaratha and the mourning palace in Ayodhyā. He worried the king would not survive the night. At dawn, the brothers matted their hair into jaṭā, donned bark clothing, and crossed the Bhāgīrathī river. They then entered the deep forest with Sītā, armed and keeping watch.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकाशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Guha describes Rāma's first night in the forest.
chapters.es: Bharata collapses like a wounded elephant upon hearing of his brother’s exile. Kauśalyā consoles him. Recovering, Bharata asks Guha for details of Rāma’s first night in the wild. Guha explains how Rāma refused all food to observe kṣatriya vows, drinking only water and sleeping on darbha grass beneath an inguḍī tree. He describes how Lakṣmaṇa stood guard with his bow drawn, protecting the camp throughout the night while others watched.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे द्व्यशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata finds Rāma's forest bed and makes a vow.
chapters.es: Bharata reaches the inguḍī tree and examines the grass where Rāma slept. He identifies golden specks from Sītā’s jewelry and threads caught in the brush. Distressed that a prince born to luxury now rests on hard earth, Bharata pledges to adopt a life of bark garments and matted hair. He resolves to stay in the forest himself so Rāma can return to rule Ayodhyā. He intends to plead until the rightful order is restored.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे त्र्यशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata’s army crosses the Gaṅgā for Prayāga.
chapters.es: At daybreak, Bharata asks Guha to ferry the host across the river. The Niṣāda king assembles five hundred boats, including flagged svastika vessels. Vasiṣṭha and the royal mothers board first, followed by the army and its treasures. Elephants swim like mountains while soldiers cross on rafts or by hand. After burning their temporary shelters, the army reaches the forest of Prayāga. Bharata then sets out with his priests to visit the sage Bharadvāja.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे चतुरशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata meets Bharadvāja and clarifies his loyalty.
chapters.es: Bharata halts his army and enters the hermitage on foot, wearing simple kṣauma silk. He follows Vasiṣṭha to meet Bharadvāja, who receives them with arghya and pādya. The sage questions Bharata’s intentions, fearing he seeks to harm Rāma. Bharata weeps, disavowing his mother’s actions and declaring his desire to restore Rāma to power. Satisfied by his loyalty, Bharadvāja reveals Rāma’s retreat at Citrakūṭa and invites the prince to rest.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे पञ्चाशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sage Bharadvāja hosts the army with a divine feast.
chapters.es: Sage Bharadvāja invokes Viśvakarman to construct a celestial palace for the army. Rivers of pāyasa and wine flow through leveled grounds while Gandharvas sing and Apsaras dance. Thousands of women provide baths to the soldiers. The troops feast on meats and rice served in golden vessels, eventually losing their desire to return home. As the sun rises, the divine assembly and magical landscape vanish, leaving the army refreshed after their night in the conjured paradise.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे षडशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata leads his army toward Citrakūṭa.
chapters.es: Bharata asks the sage Bharadvāja for the path to Rāma. The sage points toward mount Citrakūṭa and the Mandākinī river, three and a half yojanas away. Before marching, Bharata identifies his mothers. He praises Kauśalyā and Sumitrā but blames Kaikeyī for the king’s death. Bharadvāja counsels him not to fault her, as the exile serves a future purpose. The army then moves south, their chariots frightening the forest birds as they travel.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे सप्ताशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata reaches Citrakūṭa and searches for Rāma.
chapters.es: Bharata’s fourfold army advances toward Citrakūṭa, scattering herds of elephants and dappled gazelles. Recognizing the Mandākinī river and the flowering ridges described by the sage Bharadvāja, Bharata orders his troops to halt. Soldiers spot a column of smoke rising from the forest. Believing Rāma is near, Bharata instructs the army to remain behind while he proceeds toward the fire with Vasiṣṭha and Sumantra.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे अष्टाशीतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma describes the beauty of Citrakūṭa to Sītā.
chapters.es: Rāma guides Sītā through the peaks of Citrakūṭa, pointing out slopes rich in silver and madder-red minerals. He compares the mountain to a rutting elephant with waterfalls flowing like its fluid. Birds and predators roam among flowering mango and bilva trees. Rāma observes the abandoned lotus garlands of Vidyādhara lovers and glowing medicinal herbs that shine like fire at night. Living here with Lakṣmaṇa, he finds forest life more delightful than his lost kingdom.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकोननवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma describes the Mandākinī river to Sītā.
chapters.es: Rāma descends the mountain with Sītā to show her the Mandākinī river. He points out the sandbanks where geese and swans gather. Ascetics in bark garments perform morning ablutions while munis stand with arms raised toward the sun. Cakravāka birds land on floating blossoms shaken from the heights of Citrakūṭa. Rāma tells Sītā that this landscape, where elephants and lions drink, brings him more peace than his lost kingdom in Ayodhyā.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे नवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa identifies Bharata's army and prepares for combat.
chapters.es: A cloud of dust and the flight of animals alert Rāma to an approaching force. Climbing a śāla tree to investigate, Lakṣmaṇa sights a vast army. Identifying the kovidāra tree banner of Bharata, he urges Rāma to arm himself and hide Sītā in a cave. Enraged by the perceived threat, Lakṣmaṇa vows to slay his brother and his kin, comparing his coming wrath to a fire consuming a thicket.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकनवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma calms Lakṣmaṇa as the army settles.
chapters.es: Rāma pacifies Lakṣmaṇa, defending Bharata’s arrival and offering to ask that the kingdom be given to Lakṣmaṇa. Ashamed, Lakṣmaṇa descends from a śāla tree and identifies the royal elephant, Śatruñjaya. To avoid disturbing the forest, Bharata orders his assembly to encamp around the base of Citrakūṭa mountain. The army spreads across a distance of one and a half yojanas, waiting quietly as they prepare to meet Rāma.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे द्विनवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata finds Rāma's forest home on Mount Citrakūṭa.
chapters.es: Bharata orders his troops to encamp and sends Śatrughna with hunters to search the woods. Vowing not to rest until he touches the feet of Rāma and restores him to the throne, he enters the forest on foot. He walks through flowering śāla trees on the slopes of Citrakūṭa. Upon sighting a column of smoke, he identifies the location of the hermitage. Leaving his army behind, he rejoices and hurries toward the fire with Guha.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे त्रिनवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata finds Rāma living as an ascetic.
chapters.es: Bharata tracks Rāma through the forest, following signs of smoke and bark garments hanging from trees. He reaches a thatched hut where he finds Rāma seated on the ground in a vīrāsana posture. Rāma’s body is covered in dust, and his hair is bound in jaṭā. Distressed by the sight of his brother’s ascetic lifestyle, Bharata falls at Rāma’s feet in tears. Śatrughna joins him, and Rāma embraces both brothers.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे चतुर्नवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma questions Bharata about the duties of a king.
chapters.es: Rāma embraces Bharata and questions him on the administration of Ayodhyā. He asks if the prince honors the sage Vasiṣṭha and selects wise ministers. The inquiry covers military readiness, the timely payment of wages, and the protection of farmers. Rāma stresses the secrecy of state counsel and fair justice. He warns against the fourteen rājadoṣas, while urging Bharata to balance the pursuits of dharma, artha, and kāma.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे पञ्चनवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma performs funeral rites for his father.
chapters.es: Rāma collapses upon hearing of his father’s death. He leads his brothers and Sītā to the Mandākinī river to perform funeral libations, offering a piṇḍa of inguḍī pulp and badarī fruit. Their wailing echoes through the mountains, guiding the distant army and citizens to the forest retreat. As the crowds arrive, Rāma receives the weeping people, embracing his subjects and kin according to their rank.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे षण्णवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: The queens reunite with Rāma at the hermitage.
chapters.es: Vasiṣṭha leads Daśaratha’s widows to the Mandākinī river. Kauśalyā discovers a humble piṇḍa of iṅgudī pulp offered by Rāma for his father and weeps at the king’s diet. At the hermitage, the mothers embrace Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, brushing dust from their skin. Kauśalyā grieves over Sītā’s face. Rāma bows to Vasiṣṭha, while Bharata joins them with folded palms. Surrounded by ministers, the three brothers sit together like the three sacred fires.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे सप्तनवतितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata asks Rāma to return and rule.
chapters.es: Bharata inform Rāma of their father’s death. He explains that Kaikeyī’s actions caused the king's passing and begs Rāma to return for his abhiṣeka. Bharata prostrates himself, offering the throne back to his elder brother. Rāma refuses the crown, citing the necessity of honoring their father’s word. He instructs Bharata to rule the kingdom while he fulfills his fourteen-year exile in the daṇḍakāraṇya.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे शततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Jābāli urges Rāma to stop his exile and rule.
chapters.es: Jābāli rejects Rāma’s commitment to his father’s vow, calling family bonds temporary associations similar to travelers sharing an inn. He dismisses śrāddha offerings and Vedic sacrifices as a waste of resources, asserting that the dead do not consume food. Denying the reality of an afterlife, he encourages Rāma to prioritize what is perceptible and ignore unseen religious obligations. He concludes by urging Rāma to return to Ayodhyā and accept the sovereignty offered by Bharata.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकाधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma explains his refusal to return.
chapters.es: Rāma rejects the suggestion to abandon his exile for the throne. He calls satya the foundation of the world and the path to heaven. Arguing that subjects mirror their leader’s conduct, he refuses to break his promise to his father out of greed or delusion. He commits to his life in the forest, offering roots, flowers, and fruits to the ancestors. By upholding his word, he follows the path of the sages and deities who value truth.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे द्व्यधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Vasiṣṭha recounts the Ikṣvāku lineage.
chapters.es: Vasiṣṭha calms Rāma’s anger by recounting the origins of the Ikṣvāku lineage. He traces the family from the creator Brahmā and the sun deity Vivasvān down to the first king in Ayodhyā. He names ancestors such as Sagara, who dug the ocean, and Bhagīratha, noting their deeds. Finally, he identifies Rāma as the eldest heir of Daśaratha. He insists that according to the family tradition, the firstborn must govern the earth and protect the people.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे त्र्यधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma refuses Bharata’s offer to serve his exile.
chapters.es: Vasiṣṭha urges Rāma to return, citing the authority of parents and teachers. Rāma refuses, arguing that a father’s care is an unrepayable debt. Bharata spreads kuśa grass to sit in protest, but Rāma reminds him that such vows belong to priests, not kings. When Bharata offers to take Rāma’s place in the forest for fourteen years, Rāma rejects the substitution. He maintains that his father’s commands regarding the exile are final and must be fulfilled.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे चतुरधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata accepts Rāma's sandals to govern.
chapters.es: Sages and celestial beings witness the brothers' meeting, urging Bharata to uphold his father’s vow by letting Rāma stay in the forest. Bharata pleads for Rāma’s return, comparing the people’s need to farmers waiting for rain. Rāma refuses to return, declaring that the moon might lose its light before he breaks a promise. Rāma steps into gold-decorated pāduke and gives them to Bharata. Bharata places the sandals upon a royal elephant and departs while Rāma returns to his hut.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे पञ्चाधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata returns to Ayodhyā with Rāma's sandals.
chapters.es: Bharata carries the gold-decked sandals (pāduke) on his head, departing Citrakūṭa. At the hermitage of Bharadvāja, he explains Rāma's commitment to remain in the forest. After crossing the Yamunā and Gaṅgā, the procession enters Ayodhyā through Śṛṅgaverapura. Bharata finds the capital transformed into a joyless, silent shambles. He describes the city as a lightless and broken place, grieving for its desolate state in Rāma's absence.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे षडधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata finds Ayodhyā silent and grieving.
chapters.es: Bharata enters Ayodhyā in a chariot, observing a city darkened by Rāma’s exile. The streets are silent, lacking the usual gīta and vāditra. No scents of agaru or flower garlands drift through the air. He passes shuttered shops and empty highways, likening the city to a mountain stream dried by heat or a star fallen from the sky. Finally, he enters the royal palace, which feels as desolate as a mountain cave abandoned by its lion.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे सप्ताधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Bharata rules from Nandigrāma.
chapters.es: Bharata leaves Ayodhyā for Nandigrāma, carrying Rāma’s gold-decorated pāduke upon his head. Accompanied by Śatrughna and the army, he adopts the ascetic life, wearing bark garments and jaṭā. He views the kingdom as a trust and consecrates the sandals as the reigning authority. Living in Nandigrāma, he reports all administrative matters to the pāduke, holding the royal parasol and fan over them as he awaits his brother’s return from the forest.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे अष्टाधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sages flee the forest to escape rākṣasa attacks.
chapters.es: Following Bharata’s departure, Rāma observes the ascetics of Citrakūṭa whispering in fear. The chief hermit explains that the rākṣasa Khara and his followers from Janasthāna are terrorizing the settlement. These demons defile sacrifices with filth, break ritual vessels, and kill practitioners. Seeking safety, the sages resolve to move to a distant forest. Rāma pays his respects as the group departs. Despite the warning of danger, he returns to his dwelling and remains in the forest.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे नवाधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma visits Sage Atri and Sītā meets Anasūyā.
chapters.es: Rāma departs Citrakūṭa with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa to seek a new dwelling. They reach the hermitage of Sage Atri, who introduces his aged wife, Anasūyā. Known for her penance and power over nature, the ascetic receives Sītā with warmth. Anasūyā commends Sītā for choosing the forest over palace luxury. She instructs the princess on the virtues of a pativratā, explaining that a husband remains a woman’s highest refuge and primary deity.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे दशाधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sītā recounts her marriage to Anasūyā.
chapters.es: Sītā affirms her devotion to Rāma. Anasūyā grants her divine garments, jewelry, and an aṅgarāga ointment that never fades. At the ascetic's request, Sītā recounts her origin as a child found in a ploughed field by King Janaka. She describes the assembly where Rāma lifted and broke the heavy bow of Varuṇa, leading to their marriage and the union of her sister Ūrmilā with Lakṣmaṇa.

chapters.name: अयोध्याकाण्डे एकादशाधिकशततमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: The exiles depart the hermitage for the dense forest.
chapters.es: Anasūyā listens to Sītā recount her svayaṃvara as the sun sets. Sages return from their baths with wet bark-robes, and smoke from agnihotra fires rises through the trees. After receiving divine ornaments and garments from the ascetic, Sītā returns to Rāma. The group spends the night among the practitioners. At dawn, the ascetics warn of rākṣasa threats and point toward a safe path. Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā then depart into the forest.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे प्रथमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma meets forest sages and receives their hospitality.
chapters.es: Rāma enters the Daṇḍaka forest and encounters a settlement of hermitages. He unstrings his bow before approaching the ascetics, who wear bark garments and maintain sacrificial fires. The sages welcome Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa with water, wild roots, and fruits. They identify Rāma as their protector and declare that they live like children under his care. Amidst the sound of brahmaghoṣa, the forest dwellers offer hospitality and recognize his royal authority even in exile.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्वितीयः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: The demon Virādha seizes Sītā in the forest.
chapters.es: Rāma enters the dense forest at sunrise with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā. A mountain-sized demon named Virādha confronts them, wearing blood-drenched tiger skin and carrying a spit impaling slaughtered lions. He seizes Sītā, threatening the brothers. Rāma laments that Kaikeyī’s desires are now fulfilled and fears for his wife’s safety. Lakṣmaṇa, enraged, vows to slay the giant. He draws his bow, likening his strike to a thunderbolt that will leave the demon’s blood for the earth to drink.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे तृतीयः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma kills Virādha and breaks his curse.
chapters.es: Virādha confronts Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, claiming invulnerability granted by Brahmā. Rāma shatters the demon’s burning spike and pierces his body with seven golden-feathered arrows. Once the brothers break his shoulders, the creature reveals his identity as the gandharva Tumburu, cursed by Kubera. He explains that death at Rāma's hands provides his release. Rāma buries the body in a deep avaṭa to ensure the spirit’s return to heaven, then continues toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुर्थः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma witnesses Śarabhaṅga entering the sacrificial fire.
chapters.es: Rāma reaches the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and witnesses Indra departing on a sun-like chariot. The sage explains he delayed his journey to Brahmaloka to greet Rāma. Declining an offer of spiritual merit, Rāma requests a forest dwelling and receives directions to the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa. Śarabhaṅga then offers oblations and enters a sacrificial fire. He sheds his aged skin like a serpent, emerges in a youthful body, and ascends to the realm of the creator.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sages ask Rāma for protection from rākṣasas.
chapters.es: Groups of vaikhānasa and vālakhilya ascetics gather around Rāma to report the slaughter of forest-dwellers. These sages, who subsist on air or water, lead Rāma toward the Pampā and Mandākinī rivers to view the remains of those killed by rākṣasa. They remind him that a king earns merit by protecting his subjects. Rāma pledges to destroy the night-stalking demons and departs with Lakṣmaṇa for the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षष्ठः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma visits Sutīkṣṇa and declines his spiritual gifts.
chapters.es: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā reach the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa after crossing a wide river. The sage, marked by his matted jaṭā, offers Rāma the heavenly worlds won through his long tapas. Rāma declines the gift, seeking instead a dwelling where he can earn his own merit. When Sutīkṣṇa describes the fearless herds of animals nearby, Rāma worries his arrows would violate the hermitage's peace. After performing sandhyā prayers, the travelers accept a meal of forest fare and rest.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: The exiles leave Sutīkṣṇa for the forest.
chapters.es: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā wake at dawn to bathe in lily-scented water. After worshipping the sun and fire, they ask Sutīkṣṇa for permission to visit other hermitages within the daṇḍakāraṇya. Sutīkṣṇa embraces the brothers and describes the flowering forests and calm lakes they will encounter. Before leaving, Sītā hands them their quivers, bows, and swords. The brothers circumambulate the sage and depart into the woods before the sun grows hot.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sītā advises Rāma against unprovoked violence.
chapters.es: Sītā cautions Rāma against unprovoked violence as they enter the Daṇḍaka forest. She warns that carrying a bow draws a kṣatriya toward combat. She recounts the story of an ancient ascetic who guarded a sword for Indra; constant contact with the metal corrupted his mind and led him to a violent end. Sītā urges her husband to follow the peaceful dharma of a forest hermit over the duties of a warrior until their exile concludes and they return to Ayodhyā.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे नवमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma justifies using weapons to protect sages.
chapters.es: Rāma explains to Sītā that a kṣatriya carries a bow to silence the cries of the distressed. He recounts how the sages of the Daṇḍaka forest sought his protection against man-eating rākṣasas who disrupt their rituals. Although the ascetics possess the power to curse their tormentors, they refuse to exhaust their accumulated tapas. Rāma declares his devotion to satya, vowing to protect the forest dwellers even at the cost of his life. Carrying his bow, he proceeds into the groves.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे दशमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma travels for ten years to find Agastya.
chapters.es: Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa trek through forests and past the Pañcāpsara lake, where music from an underwater dwelling built for five apsaras echoes across the lotuses. Over ten years, they move between hermitages before Rāma asks Sutīkṣṇa for the path to Agastya’s home. On the journey, Rāma describes how Agastya once devoured and digested the demon Vātāpi. They finally reach a grove defined by sacrificial smoke and hanging bark garments, where Rāma prepares to meet the sage.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकादशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Agastya welcomes Rāma and gives him divine weapons.
chapters.es: Lakṣmaṇa requests an audience through a disciple, who leads the travelers into Agastya’s presence. The sage provides water and forest food, fulfilling the duties of a host to a visiting king. Agastya then entrusts Rāma with a golden bow of Viṣṇu made by Viśvakarman, a celestial arrow, two inexhaustible quivers, and a gold-adorned sword. These divine weapons, formerly used by the gods to defeat demons, are given to Rāma to ensure his triumph over his enemies.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्वादशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Agastya directs the exiles to live in Pañcavaṭī.
chapters.es: Agastya welcomes the travelers and acknowledges their fatigue. He praises Sītā for her loyalty, likening her to the constant Arundhatī rather than the fickle nature of lightning or wind. When Rāma asks for a place to build an āśrama, the sage directs him to Pañcavaṭī near the Godāvarī river. He describes a path leading north through madhuka trees to a large banyan. Taking their bows and quivers, the brothers pay respects to the sage and depart with Sītā for the new forest home.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रयोदशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma meets Jaṭāyu, who offers to protect Sītā.
chapters.es: While traveling toward Pañcavaṭī, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa encounter the vulture Jaṭāyu perched upon a tree. After identifying himself as a friend of King Daśaratha, Jaṭāyu recounts the lineage of all creatures, tracing life from the daughters of Dakṣa and the sage Kaśyapa. He details the origins of deities, demons, humans, and animals before identifying himself as the son of Aruṇa. Jaṭāyu pledges to guard Sītā within the forest. Rāma embraces the bird and continues his journey with this new ally.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुर्दशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa builds a parṇaśālā at Pañcavaṭī.
chapters.es: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā reach the flowering forests of Pañcavaṭī. Rāma identifies a level site near the Godāvarī river for their hermitage. Lakṣmaṇa constructs a parṇaśālā using mud, bamboo, and leaves. After bathing and performing a puṣpabali with lotuses, he presents the shelter to Rāma. Rāma embraces his brother and compares Lakṣmaṇa to their father, Daśaratha. The trio settles near the bird Jaṭāyu, living among the groves and mineral-streaked mountains.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चदशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa describes the winter season.
chapters.es: Winter settles over the forest as Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā walk to the Godāvarī river for morning ablutions. Lakṣmaṇa describes the landscape of frozen dew, golden rice stalks, and the moon blurred by mist. He grieves for Bharata, who practices austerities on the cold earth of Ayodhyā. When Lakṣmaṇa speaks harshly of Kaikeyī, Rāma silences the criticism while praising his brother's devotion. After bathing, they offer water libations to their ancestors and recite prayers to the sun.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षोडशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śūrpaṇakhā proposes marriage to Rāma.
chapters.es: After bathing in the Godāvarī, Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa return to their parṇaśālā. While they rest, the demoness Śūrpaṇakhā approaches. Struck by Rāma’s beauty, she contrasts his form with her own. She identifies herself as the sister of Rāvaṇa and describes her powerful brothers. Śūrpaṇakhā offers herself as a wife, threatening to devour Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa so she and Rāma may roam the forests together. Rāma listens to her proposal and begins his reply with a smile.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तदशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa mutilates Śūrpaṇakhā for attacking Sītā.
chapters.es: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa deflect the advances of the rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā with mocking humor. When the demoness interprets their jests as truth, she attempts to kill Sītā to secure Rāma for herself. Rāma halts the playfulness and instructs Lakṣmaṇa to punish her. Lakṣmaṇa draws his sword and severs her nose and ears. Covered in blood, Śūrpaṇakhā roars and flees the leaf-thatched hut, eventually reaching her brother Khara in Janasthāna to report the assault.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टादशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Khara sends fourteen warriors against Rāma.
chapters.es: Śūrpaṇakhā arrives before Khara, disfigured and soaked in blood. Infuriated, Khara vows to kill her attackers, imagining vultures devouring their flesh and the earth drinking their foamy blood. Śūrpaṇakhā identifies Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, dressed in cīra and kṛṣṇājina, and describes the woman staying with them. Seeking revenge, she asks to drink their blood. Khara dispatches fourteen demons to the daṇḍakāraṇya to slaughter the exiles and satisfy his sister’s wish.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकोनविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma kills the fourteen demon warriors.
chapters.es: Śūrpaṇakhā leads fourteen demons to the leaf-thatched hermitage where Rāma sits with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. Rāma instructs Lakṣmaṇa to protect Sītā before stringing his gold-decorated bow. When the demons hurl their spears, Rāma shatters them mid-air and retaliates with fourteen gold-feathered nārāca arrows. The projectiles pierce the demons' chests, causing them to fall like uprooted trees. Covered in blood, Śūrpaṇakhā flees to her brother Khara to report the slaughter of her retinue.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे विंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śūrpaṇakhā incites Khara to avenge the demons.
chapters.es: Śūrpaṇakhā returns to Khara, weeping and rolling on the ground like a serpent. She reports that Rāma’s arrows destroyed the fourteen rākṣasa warriors sent to protect her. Describing her fear as an ocean filled with crocodiles, she demands Khara kill the human brothers. She mocks Khara’s reputation, calling his strength a lie. Unless he defeats the enemy in the daṇḍakāraṇya, she vows to end her life, urging him to flee Janasthāna before Rāma’s power consumes him.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Khara leads an army of demons to Janasthāna.
chapters.es: Khara vows to slay Rāma and commands his general, Dūṣaṇa, to mobilize fourteen thousand rākṣasa warriors from Janasthāna. These soldiers carry axes, spears, and spiked clubs. Khara mounts a golden chariot adorned with jewels, sun motifs, and bells. As the army marches with a deafening roar, the charioteer spurs the horses forward. Khara leads the charge, sounding like a storm cloud raining stones as he rushes to confront his enemy in the forest.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्वाविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Khara ignores ill omens before the battle.
chapters.es: As Khara’s army marches toward Janasthāna, dark clouds rain blood. Horses stumble on the highway while a vulture perches upon the golden flagstaff. The sun appears encircled by a blood-red ring, and the demon Rāhu causes an untimely eclipse. Jackals breathe fire and the earth trembles, yet Khara dismisses these utpāta or ill omens. He boasts of his invincibility before leading his commanders to surround Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, as gods gather to watch.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रयोविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma prepares to fight the demon army alone.
chapters.es: Blood-red clouds and smoking arrows signal an imminent slaughter. Rāma sends Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā to a mountain cave, then dons his armor and strings his gold-plated bow. Fourteen thousand demons under Khara advance with banners and drums, causing forest animals to flee. Rāma stands alone as the army nears like a rising sea. He summons his anger for the coming carnage, appearing like the god Pinākin ready to destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुर्विंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma decimates the rākṣasa front lines.
chapters.es: Khara arrives at the hermitage and orders his charioteer to charge the solitary Rāma. A massive host of demons surrounds him, unleashing a storm of spears, swords, and iron hammers. Rāma stands firm, absorbing the blows like a mountain struck by lightning. He bends his bow into a circle, releasing thousands of heron-feathered arrows that pierce bodies and light up the sky. After Rāma decimates the front lines, Dūṣaṇa rallies the survivors for a second assault.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma kills Dūṣaṇa and the demon army.
chapters.es: Rāma withstands a shower of stones before retaliating with gold-tipped arrows. He severs the arms of Dūṣaṇa, whose iron parigha falls like a broken banner. After striking down the commanders Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, and Pramāthī, Rāma eliminates fourteen thousand warriors. The forest floor becomes a mire of flesh and blood, resembling a sacrificial altar strewn with kuśa grass. Only Khara and Triśiras remain to face the human archer who stands alone.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षड्विंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma slays Triśiras in single combat.
chapters.es: Triśiras asks Khara for permission to duel Rāma. Advancing in a chariot, the three-headed demon strikes Rāma’s forehead with three arrows. Rāma likens the impact to falling flowers and retaliates by killing the horses and charioteer. He pierces the demon's chest and severs the three heads of Triśiras with sharp shafts. As the surviving rākṣasa forces flee like deer from a tiger, Khara stops their retreat and charges toward Rāma to continue the battle himself.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma destroys Khara’s chariot and bow.
chapters.es: Following the deaths of Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras, Khara charges Rāma from a golden chariot. Their exchange of arrows thickens the air, obscuring the sun. Khara shatters Rāma’s bow and pierces his armor, drawing blood. Rāma strings the vaiṣṇava bow and systematically destroys Khara’s equipment. He kills the horses, beheads the charioteer, and splinters Khara's bow with precise shafts. Khara leaps to the ground with a mace as gods and sages gather.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टाविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma and Khara exchange words before their duel.
chapters.es: Rāma confronts the chariotless Khara, denouncing his slaughter of ascetics in the daṇḍakāraṇya. He warns that the fruits of sin arrive like seasonal flowers or slow-acting poison. Khara mocks Rāma's self-praise and compares himself to an unshakeable mountain. He hurls a flaming mace that incinerates nearby shrubs. Rāma meets the weapon with a volley of arrows, shattering it in mid-air. The broken mace falls to the earth like a serpent rendered harmless by a charm.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकोनत्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma kills Khara with a celestial arrow.
chapters.es: Rāma shatters Khara’s mace and mocks the demon’s empty boasts. Enraged, Khara uproots a sāla tree and hurls it, but Rāma splinters the trunk with arrows. When the demon charges, Rāma releases a celestial shaft granted by Indra. The arrow strikes Khara’s chest, causing him to fall like Vṛtra. Sages rejoice that the Daṇḍaka forest is finally secure. Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa emerge from a mountain cave, and Sītā embraces her victorious husband in the hermitage.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śūrpaṇakhā informs Rāvaṇa of Khara's death.
chapters.es: Śūrpaṇakhā witnesses the deaths of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, Triśiras, and fourteen thousand demon warriors, then flees to Laṅkā to seek Rāvaṇa. The king sits on a golden throne, his ten heads and twenty arms bearing scars from the cakra of Viṣṇu and the tusks of Airāvata. He possesses the seized Puṣpaka chariot, disrupts sacred sacrifices, and holds a boon of invincibility against all beings except humans. Displaying her disfigured face, Śūrpaṇakhā approaches her brother to report Rāma’s victory.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकत्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śūrpaṇakhā rebukes Rāvaṇa for his negligence.
chapters.es: Śūrpaṇakhā confronts Rāvaṇa amidst his ministers, criticizing his obsession with pleasure and lack of cāra, or spies. She reports that Rāma has slaughtered fourteen thousand demons, including Khara and Dūṣaṇa, in Janasthāna. Comparing an inattentive king to a discarded garment or a dry log, she warns of his impending ruin. Rāvaṇa sits in silence, pondering the loss of his army and the harsh critique of his failures as a ruler.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्वात्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śūrpaṇakhā incites Rāvaṇa to abduct Sītā.
chapters.es: Śūrpaṇakhā describes Rāma to Rāvaṇa as a warrior dressed in bark and deerskin who wields a gold-banded bow. She recounts how he decimated fourteen thousand demons in the daṇḍakāraṇya with arrows like venomous snakes. She details the virtues of Lakṣmaṇa and the beauty of Sītā, a princess of Videha. Claiming her disfigurement happened while trying to secure the woman for her brother, she incites Rāvaṇa to kill the brothers and take Sītā for himself.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रयस्त्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa travels to find Mārīca.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa departs in a golden chariot yoked with donkey-faced beasts. He flies over the sea's edge, passing groves of sāla and tāla trees and ponds filled with lotuses. He observes aerial chariots, forests of sandalwood, and heaps of pearls on the shore. He reaches a massive banyan tree called Subhadra, where Garuḍa once saved sages while carrying a giant elephant and tortoise. Crossing the ocean, Rāvaṇa finds the demon Mārīca living as an ascetic in a secluded hermitage.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुस्त्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa asks Mārīca to manifest as a deer.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa arrives at Mārīca’s dwelling seeking refuge after Rāma destroys fourteen thousand demons in Janasthāna. Describing Rāma as a cruel outcaste, Rāvaṇa details the mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā and his plan to seize Sītā. He instructs Mārīca to manifest as a golden deer dappled with silver spots to lure Sītā from her hut. Once she is isolated, Rāvaṇa intends to snatch her away like Rāhu eclipsing the moon. Recognition of Rāma’s power leaves Mārīca paralyzed with fear.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चत्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Mārīca warns Rāvaṇa of Rāma’s righteousness.
chapters.es: Mārīca warns Rāvaṇa that while many offer pleasing speech, few listen to beneficial but harsh truths. He describes Rāma as vigrahavān dharmaḥ, a man who entered the Daṇḍaka forest to uphold his father’s honor. Using fire imagery, Mārīca likens Rāma’s bow to a gaping mouth and his arrows to consuming flames. He cautions that a ruler driven by lust destroys his people and urges Rāvaṇa to consult ministers like Vibhīṣaṇa to assess the strength of their enemy.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षट्त्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Mārīca recounts his first defeat by Rāma.
chapters.es: Mārīca describes his past as a mountain-sized demon terrorizing the Daṇḍaka forest. When the sage Viśvāmitra sought protection, the young Rāma guarded the sacrificial altar with his bow. Despite his youth and knotted śikhā hair, Rāma struck the demon with an arrow, hurling him a hundred yojanas into the ocean. Mārīca warns Rāvaṇa that pursuing Sītā will bring ruin to Laṅkā, urging the king to avoid Rāma’s arrows to save his people.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तत्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Mārīca describes his paralyzing fear of Rāma.
chapters.es: Mārīca recalls returning to the Daṇḍaka forest disguised as a sharp-horned beast to prey upon ascetics. When he charges the exiled Rāma to avenge a past defeat, three arrows whistle from a heavy bow, killing his companions and sparing him only by flight. Now living as a recluse, Mārīca is consumed by terror, seeing the deerskin-clad warrior in every tree and shadow. Even the sound of the syllable ra in words like ratna or ratha triggers a fear of the coming death-noose.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टात्रिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa commands Mārīca to assist him.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa rejects the warning of his counselor, likening the advice to seeds sown in barren soil. Driven by his resolve to seize Sītā, he commands Mārīca to transform into a māyāmṛga, a golden deer dappled with silver. He demands that the demon lure Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa away from their hermitage through this deception. Asserting his royal authority, Rāvaṇa threatens Mārīca with death for further dissent, offering him half his kingdom for his cooperation.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकोनचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Mārīca foretells the ruin of the rākṣasas.
chapters.es: Mārīca confronts Rāvaṇa with harsh truths, questioning which advisor seeks the king’s ruin. He warns that a kingdom governed by a cruel leader perishes like sheep guarded by a jackal. Mārīca describes the impending destruction of the rākṣasa race and the fall of Laṅkā. He compares Rāvaṇa’s ministers to a slow charioteer driving swift horses into a pit. Foreseeing his death as a kākatālīya or unexpected disaster, Mārīca insists that Sītā’s abduction signals the end for them all.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Mārīca transforms into an illusory deer.
chapters.es: Mārīca yields to Rāvaṇa's demands and boards a gem-encrusted chariot. They fly over cities and mountains, arriving at the Daṇḍaka forest near Rāma's hermitage. Mārīca transforms into a māyāmṛga, an illusory deer with silver-spotted skin and hooves of vaidūrya. He prances through the greenery to attract Sītā’s attention. While gathering flowers among the trees, Sītā discovers the glittering creature and watches its movements with amazement.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma pursues the illusory deer.
chapters.es: Sītā spots a deer with a golden and silver body while gathering flowers. Drawn to its gem-like spots, she asks Rāma to capture the animal or bring its skin to their hermitage. Lakṣmaṇa warns that the creature is the demon Mārīca employing māyā, but Rāma is attracted by its appearance. Recalling how Agastya destroyed Vātāpi, Rāma resolves to hunt the beast. He instructs Lakṣmaṇa and Jaṭāyu to guard Sītā while he pursues the golden antelope with his bow.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्विचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma kills Mārīca and suspects a trap.
chapters.es: Rāma fastens a golden-hilted sword and tracks the illusory deer through the forest. The creature lures him away, vanishing and reappearing like the moon amidst clouds. Rāma eventually looses a blazing arrow that pierces the heart of the beast. As the demon Mārīca sheds his animal form, he cries out for Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa in Rāma’s own voice. Realizing the deception, a fearful Rāma kills a real deer for meat and hastens back toward Janasthāna.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रिचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sītā sends Lakṣmaṇa into the forest.
chapters.es: Hearing a pained cry resembling Rāma’s voice, Sītā urges Lakṣmaṇa to leave their forest dwelling. Lakṣmaṇa resists, explaining the sound is a demonic māyā and that Rāma remains invincible. Enraged, Sītā accuses him of hidden malice and threatens to drown herself in the Godāvarī or enter fire. Stung by her words, Lakṣmaṇa invokes the forest deities as witnesses to his integrity. He finally bows to the weeping Vaidehī and departs into the woods to find his brother.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुश्चत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa approaches Sītā in a mendicant’s disguise.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa approaches the parṇaśālā disguised as a parivrājaka in saffron robes, carrying a kamaṇḍalu and staff. Nature falls silent; the wind ceases and the Godāvarī river slows. He finds Sītā alone and praises her skin and eyes, asking if she is a goddess or a forest spirit. Mistaking the demon for a holy guest, Sītā offers a straw bṛsī and forest food. While she scans the green horizon for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, Rāvaṇa resolves to abduct her.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sītā identifies herself and rejects Rāvaṇa.
chapters.es: Sītā identifies herself to the wandering mendicant as the wife of Rāma and daughter of Janaka. She details their exile to the daṇḍakāraṇya forest following the boons granted to Kaikeyī. When the guest reveals himself as the demon king Rāvaṇa, he offers her wealth and a throne in Laṅkā. Sītā spurns his proposal, likening him to a jackal pursuing a lioness and comparing Rāma to gold against his lead. Although she trembles, she asserts her devotion before the threatening king.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षट्चत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa reveals his identity and wealth.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa reveals his identity as the brother of Kubera, boasting of his conquest of the puṣpaka chariot and his power over the sun and wind. He describes Laṅkā as a city of golden walls and vaidūrya gates, dismissing Rāma as a powerless ascetic. Driven by the arrows of Manmatha, he demands Sītā’s devotion. Sītā responds with red-eyed fury, rebuking his lack of restraint. She declares that stealing Rāma's wife ensures certain death for the rākṣasa race.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa reveals his form and seizes Sītā.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa discards his mendicant disguise to reveal his massive form. He boasts of his power to drink the oceans before seizing Sītā by her hair and thighs. Forcing her onto a golden chariot drawn by donkeys, he ascends into the sky. Sītā cries out for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, rebuking her captor’s unrighteousness. She begs the flowering karṇikāra trees, the Godāvarī river, and the vulture Jaṭāyu to inform her husband of this abduction.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टचत्वारिंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Jaṭāyu intercepts Rāvaṇa during the abduction.
chapters.es: Jaṭāyu, the vulture king, hears Sītā’s cries and intercepts Rāvaṇa. Perched atop a tree like a mountain peak, he warns the demon of the consequences of stealing another’s wife. He asserts his loyalty to Rāma and the principles of dharma. Despite his age, Jaṭāyu challenges the young, armed Rāvaṇa to combat. He compares the abduction of Vaidehī to a venomous snake hidden in one’s clothes. He promises to strike Rāvaṇa from his chariot like a ripe fruit from its stalk.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकोनपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa wounds Jaṭāyu and flees into the sky.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa pounces on Jaṭāyu, initiating a violent duel resembling the clash of clouds. Jaṭāyu wounds the demon with sharp claws and shatters his gem-studded bow and golden ratha. Despite his age, the bird severs Rāvaṇa’s ten left arms with his beak. Rāvaṇa draws a sword to cut the vulture’s wings and feet, causing him to fall to the earth. Sītā rushes to the bleeding Jaṭāyu and laments as Rāvaṇa prepares to flee into the sky with his captive.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Nature mourns as Rāvaṇa carries Sītā away.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa seizes Sītā by her hair as she clings to forest trees. He carries her into the sky, where her yellow kauśeya and gold ornaments flash against his dark body like lightning in a storm cloud. Her flower garlands, a gem-studded nūpura, and a pearl hāra fall toward the earth. Nature reacts to the abduction; mountains weep through waterfalls and animals chase her shadow. Brahmā declares the demon’s destruction certain. Sītā calls for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa as she disappears.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sītā condemns Rāvaṇa during his flight.
chapters.es: Sītā weeps and rebukes Rāvaṇa as he carries her through the sky. Her eyes redden with anger while she condemns his deceitful use of the illusory deer to lure Rāma away. She warns that he cannot survive the touch of Rāma’s arrows, which strike like forest fire. Comparing his actions to the delusions of a dying man, she describes visions of the blood-filled Vaitaraṇī river and iron-thorned trees. Despite her reminders of the demons slain at Janasthāna, the captor continues his flight.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्विपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa imprisons Sītā and sends spies to Janasthāna.
chapters.es: Sītā spots five monkeys on a mountain peak and drops her golden uttarīya and jewelry, hoping they might alert Rāma. Rāvaṇa carries her across the ocean, unmindful of the falling ornaments or the celestial voices foretelling his end. Upon reaching Laṅkā, he confines her within his inner apartments under the watch of female guards. He then commands eight demons to occupy Janasthāna and spy on Rāma. Rāvaṇa rejoices in his success, unaware he has brought his own death into the palace.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रिपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa tries to entice Sītā with his palace.
chapters.es: Rāvaṇa enters his palace to find Sītā weeping among demonesses. He leads her through the mansion, showcasing golden staircases, crystal floors, and ivory windows to entice her. Boasting of his millions of subjects and the puṣpaka chariot, he offers her the position of chief queen. He belittles Rāma as a weak ascetic and insists that no god can breach the ocean-bound Laṅkā. Despite prostrating his ten heads at her feet, his pride leads him toward inevitable death.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुःपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāvaṇa imprisons Sītā in the aśokavanikā.
chapters.es: Sītā places a blade of grass between herself and Rāvaṇa, refusing to look at him directly. She warns that Rāma, an Ikṣvāku prince, will pierce his body with golden arrows. Rāvaṇa grants her twelve months to submit before his cooks butcher her. He stamps the earth and orders hideous demonesses to lead her to the aśokavanikā. There, they attempt to break her spirit with threats and pleas. Surrounded by these captors, Sītā collapses like a doe among tigresses.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma meets Lakṣmaṇa and suspects disaster.
chapters.es: Rāma kills the demon Mārīca and hurries back toward the hermitage. A jackal howls behind him, and forest birds circle to his left, signaling disaster. Fearing that Mārīca’s mimicry lured Lakṣmaṇa away, Rāma encounters his brother on the path. He rebukes Lakṣmaṇa for leaving Sītā alone in a forest filled with demons. Distressed by a throbbing left eye and an aching heart, Rāma anticipates that Sītā has been abducted or killed by the inhabitants of Janasthāna.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षट्पञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma discovers the empty hermitage.
chapters.es: Rāma encounters Lakṣmaṇa returning alone and questions the absence of Vaidehī. He fears the rākṣasa of Janasthāna killed her in retaliation for Khara’s death. Imagining Sītā’s terror at the demon’s mimicked cry, Rāma threatens to abandon his own life. The brothers rush back to their forest dwelling, but Rāma finds the clearing silent. He wanders through the empty grove with a parched throat and sinking heart, realizing his fears of her abduction are true.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa explains his departure to Rāma.
chapters.es: Rāma meets Lakṣmaṇa on the forest path and questions why he left Sītā alone. Lakṣmaṇa explains how Mārīca mimicked Rāma’s voice, causing Sītā to panic. When Lakṣmaṇa initially refused to leave, Sītā accused him of harboring sinful intentions toward her. Stung by her harsh words, Lakṣmaṇa abandoned the hermitage. Rāma reprimands his brother for yielding to her anger and leaving Sītā vulnerable, reminding him that he should have trusted in Rāma’s invincibility against any rākṣasa.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टपञ्चाशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma searches the forest for Sītā.
chapters.es: Rāma returns to the hermitage to find the cottage empty and the kuśa grass scattered. Troubled by inauspicious omens, he wanders through the forest, pleading with the trees for news of Sītā. He questions the deer and elephants, even imagining his wife hiding behind trees to tease him. Fearing that demons have devoured her, he runs between rivers and hills, searching frantically for any sign of her among the flowering trees and mountain streams.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकोनषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma searches for Sītā in despair.
chapters.es: Rāma returns to find the parṇaśālā empty and its grass mats scattered. He calls into the trees, pleading with Vaidehī to end her perceived game of hide-and-seek. Mourning among tearful fawns, he fears the judgment of his late father for failing his vows. Lakṣmaṇa urges him to search the mountain caves and lotus ponds. Though they traverse the daṇḍakāraṇya together, Rāma sinks into despair, losing consciousness and sighing repeatedly as he finds no trace of his wife.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma finds combat signs and threatens the world.
chapters.es: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa search the Godāvarī banks and Mount Prasravaṇa for Sītā. The river remains silent, fearing the demon king. Rāma identifies Sītā’s discarded flowers before discovering a broken golden chariot, a shattered bow, and blood on the earth. Seeing giant footprints, he fears she has been devoured. His sorrow turns to rage as he threatens to dry the oceans and release arrows that will dismantle the three worlds unless she is safely returned.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa advises Rāma against cosmic destruction.
chapters.es: Rāma stands with a strung bow, breathing like the samvartaka fire. Ready to destroy the universe, he scans the forest while Lakṣmaṇa discovers a shattered chariot and blood-soaked earth. Lakṣmaṇa urges Rāma to return to his natural prakṛti, recalling the kṣamā of the earth. He argues against punishing all creatures for one person’s crime. They must search the mountains and oceans first. Lakṣmaṇa vows to find the abductor, advising Rāma to use force only if diplomacy fails.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे द्विषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa consoles Rāma and urges action.
chapters.es: Lakṣmaṇa presses the feet of his grieving brother to rouse his clouded intellect. He argues that if the unshakeable earth trembles and the sun faces eclipses, no mortal or god can escape fate. Citing the losses of the sage Vasiṣṭha and King Yayāti, he urges Rāma to abandon despair. He calls on Rāma to refrain from destroying the entire world and instead focus his prowess on identifying and punishing the specific sinner who abducted Sītā.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे त्रिषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma finds the dying Jaṭāyu.
chapters.es: Rāma searches the Janasthāna forest and finds the vulture Jaṭāyu fallen on the earth, drenched in blood. Initially suspecting the bird of devouring Sītā, Rāma prepares his bow to strike. Jaṭāyu speaks with failing breath, revealing that Rāvaṇa abducted the princess and severed his wings during their battle. Rāma sees the demon’s broken chariot and weapons nearby. Overcome by grief, he embraces the dying bird, mourning the loss of his father’s friend and the misfortune of his exile.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे चतुःषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma performs funeral rites for Jaṭāyu.
chapters.es: Rāma finds Jaṭāyu bleeding on the forest floor. With his final breaths, the bird reveals that Rāvaṇa abducted Sītā during the vinda muhūrta and fled toward the south. After Jaṭāyu dies, Rāma mourns him like a father and builds a funeral pyre. He cremates the bird with sacred fire, offers portions of deer meat on the grass, and recites funeral prayers. The brothers then perform water libations in the Godāvarī river to ensure the bird's passage to a heavenly state.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे पञ्चषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa encounter Kabandha.
chapters.es: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa travel southward through the dense krauñcāraṇya forest. While Lakṣmaṇa observes ill omens, a roar shakes the trees. They encounter Kabandha, a massive demon without a head or neck, whose single eye sits within his chest and whose mouth opens in his belly. The creature extends his long arms and seizes both brothers. Held fast, Rāma speaks of the power of kāla, noting that even the strongest warriors eventually succumb to time like sand embankments before a flood.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे षट्षष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa sever Kabandha’s limbs.
chapters.es: Kabandha traps Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa within his massive arms, claiming them as prey provided by fate. The brothers draw their swords and strike, severing the demon's limbs at the shoulders. Kabandha falls to the earth with a roar, his body drenched in blood. When he asks for their names, Lakṣmaṇa identifies them as princes of the Ikṣvāku line searching for Sītā. Remembering a prophecy by Indra, the demon welcomes them and prepares to explain his deformed state.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्तषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Kabandha explains his curse and seeks cremation.
chapters.es: The creature reveals his origin as the son of Danu, once resembling the sun. After he harassed forest seers and challenged Indra, a thunderbolt drove his head and thighs into his torso, leaving him with a mouth in his belly and arms a yojana long. He recounts the curse of Sthūlaśiras and the promise of liberation through Rāma. He urges the brothers to cremate his body in a pit before sunset, promising that his restored spirit will guide them toward Sītā.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे अष्टषष्टितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Kabandha advises Rāma to find Sugrīva.
chapters.es: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa ignite a funeral pyre for Kabandha in a mountain cave. From the burning flesh, the demon rises as a celestial figure seated upon a swan-drawn chariot. Now unburdened, he instructs Rāma to travel to Lake Pampā and form an alliance with the exiled monkey Sugrīva on Mount Ṛṣyamūka. He urges them to seal this friendship before a sacred fire. Kabandha promises that Sugrīva and his vānara followers will search the earth to locate the missing Sītā.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकोनसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Kabandha directs the brothers to Lake Pampā.
chapters.es: Kabandha directs the brothers toward the west, past trees laden with jambū and panasa fruits. He describes the clear waters of Lake Pampā, where lotuses bloom and fat birds gather. He instructs them to visit the hermitage of the ascetic Śabarī near the forest of Sage Mataṅga. Finally, he points toward Mount Ṛṣyamūka, a peak where the monkey Sugrīva hides in a stone-covered cave. After urging a pact of friendship, the celestial being shines like the sun and ascends into the sky.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे सप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Śabarī welcomes Rāma and ascends to heaven.
chapters.es: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa travel west to the banks of Lake Pampā and enter the hermitage of the ascetic Śabarī. She offers them forest fruits gathered in anticipation of their arrival, as foretold by her departed teachers. Śabarī leads the princes through the Mataṅga forest, pointing out sacrificial altars that still glow and wet bark garments that never dry. After receiving Rāma’s blessing, she consigns her body to a sacrificial fire and ascends to the celestial realm of the sages.

chapters.name: अरण्यकाण्डे एकसप्ततितमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma reaches Lake Pampā to seek Sugrīva.
chapters.es: After Śabarī’s departure, Rāma observes the Mataṅga hermitage where predators and prey coexist. Following ritual ablutions, he leads Lakṣmaṇa toward Lake Pampā and Mount Ṛṣyamūka to find the exiled monkey chief Sugrīva. They traverse forests of tilaka and aśoka trees filled with birdsong. Upon reaching the water, Rāma views the lake covered in multicolored lotuses resembling a carpet, as he prepares to seek an alliance for his search.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे प्रथमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma mourns for Sītā near Lake Pampā.
chapters.es: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa reach the shores of Lake Pampā at the start of spring. The flowering karṇikāra trees and the scent of lotuses remind Rāma of the abducted Sītā. He observes peacocks and birds, finding the cool breeze painful in his solitude. After lamenting his loss, Rāma walks toward Mount Ṛṣyamūka. Seeing the armed brothers, the resident monkeys retreat in fear and watch the strangers from the heights.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे द्वितीयः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva sends Hanumān to identify two strangers.
chapters.es: Sugrīva watches two armed men approach and retreats to a higher peak with his ministers. The monkeys leap across the ridges of Mount Ṛṣyamūka, scaring the local wildlife. Fearing the strangers are spies sent by Vālin, Sugrīva remains agitated despite Hanumān’s reassurances. He commands Hanumān to assume a humble form and engage the warriors. By studying their expressions and speech, Hanumān must determine their intentions. The counselor departs to meet them.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे तृतीयः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Hanumān meets Rāma and proposes an alliance.
chapters.es: Hanumān leaps from Mount Ṛṣyamūka to approach the brothers. Disguised as a mendicant, he asks why warriors with lotus-petal eyes and heavy bows wander the woods as ascetics. He likens their weapons to rainbows and golden serpents. Hanumān identifies himself as the son of Vāyu and minister to the exiled Sugrīva, proposing a pact of friendship. Impressed by the monkey’s speech, Rāma asks Lakṣmaṇa to respond with kindness to their visitor.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे चतुर्थः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Hanumān leads the brothers to Sugrīva.
chapters.es: Hanumān questions the brothers about their journey through the Pampā forest. Lakṣmaṇa describes Rāma’s exile from Ayodhyā and the abduction of Sītā, explaining that the demon Kabandha directed them to seek Sugrīva. Seeing that both parties suffer from lost kingdoms and stolen wives, Hanumān promises the monkey king’s assistance. The son of Vāyu then conducts the two brothers toward the summit of Mount Ṛṣyamūka to meet Sugrīva.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे पञ्चमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma and Sugrīva form an alliance by fire.
chapters.es: Hanumān travels to the Malaya mountain to introduce Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to Sugrīva. He explains Rāma’s lineage from the Ikṣvāku dynasty and the search for his abducted wife. Sugrīva sheds his fear, takes human form, and extends his hand to forge an alliance. Rāma grasps his hand and embraces him. Hanumān kindles a fire from wood, and the two allies perform a pradakṣiṇam around the flames to seal their bond as vayasya.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे षष्ठः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva shows Sītā’s ornaments to Rāma.
chapters.es: Sugrīva promises to recover Sītā. He fetches a bundle of ornaments and a silk garment from a mountain cave, which Sītā dropped while Rāvaṇa carried her away. Rāma recognizes the jewelry and collapses in grief. He presses the tokens to his chest and hisses with rage like a provoked serpent, demanding the location of the demon to exact revenge. Sugrīva remains by his side as the prince mourns.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे सप्तमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva comforts Rāma and pledges support.
chapters.es: Sugrīva offers an añjali and promises to find Maithilī. He admits he knows nothing of the demon’s lineage but urges Rāma to regain his dhṛti. The monkey shares his own experience of loss to encourage composure. Rāma wipes his tears with his garment and embraces Sugrīva. He pledges his support and vows never to speak an untruth. Hearing this, Sugrīva and his ministers feel their own goals are already achieved.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे अष्टमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva seeks help against Vālin.
chapters.es: Sugrīva affirms his alliance with Rāma. After breaking a flowering śāla branch to create a seat for Rāma, Sugrīva recounts his humiliation. He explains how his brother Vālin seized his wife and exiled him to the mountains. Rāma promises to strike Vālin with gold-decked arrows. Heartened by this vow, Sugrīva wipes away his tears and begins to detail the specific origins of their long-standing enmity.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे नवमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva recounts the conflict with Vālin.
chapters.es: The demon Māyāvin challenges Vālin to a midnight duel at the gates of Kiṣkindhā. Vālin pursues the foe into a deep cavern, commanding Sugrīva to stand guard at the entrance. After a year, blood flows from the cave. Sugrīva seals the opening with a massive stone, performs funeral rites, and accepts the crown. Vālin eventually emerges alive after slaying the demon. Seeing Sugrīva on the throne, he views the kingship as betrayal and reacts with fury.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे दशमः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva describes his exile to Rāma.
chapters.es: Sugrīva offers the royal parasol and cāmara to Vālin, but his brother rejects the peace offering. Before the ministers, Vālin recounts killing the demon Māyāvin and breaking through the boulder Sugrīva used to seal the cave. Believing his brother stole the throne, Vālin banishes him and seizes his wife, Rumā. Sugrīva flees to Mount Ṛṣyamūka. Upon hearing this, Rāma pledges to strike Vālin with sharp arrows and end Sugrīva’s exile.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे एकादशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma demonstrates his strength to Sugrīva.
chapters.es: Sugrīva recounts Vālin’s feats, describing how the monkey king once battled the buffalo demon Dundubhi. After the demon challenged the ocean and Mount Himavat, he arrived at Kiṣkindhā. Vālin seized the buffalo by the horns, struck him down, and hurled the carcass. This act led to a curse from the sage Mataṅga when blood defiled his grove. Rāma proves his strength by using his toe to flick the massive skeleton across ten yojana-s.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे द्वादशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Lakṣmaṇa marks Sugrīva with a vine.
chapters.es: Rāma pierces seven śāla trees and the mountain earth with a single arrow to prove his strength. Sugrīva challenges Vālin to a duel, but Rāma cannot distinguish the identical brothers and withholds his shot. Beaten, Sugrīva retreats. To prevent further confusion, Lakṣmaṇa ties a flowering gajapuṣpī vine around Sugrīva’s neck. Thus marked like a cloud garlanded by cranes, Sugrīva returns to the city to face his brother once more.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे त्रयोदशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma visits the Saptajana hermitage.
chapters.es: Rāma and Sugrīva travel toward Kiṣkindhā accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and the monkey leaders. Along the route, they observe wild elephants and lotus-filled tanks. Sugrīva identifies the Saptajana hermitage, where seven sages performed austerities and ascended to heaven. The site remains guarded by spiritual power, marked by the smoke of sacred fires and celestial sounds. Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa offer an añjali in reverence. The party then arrives at the city ruled by Vālin.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे चतुर्दशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Sugrīva challenges Vālin at Kiṣkindhā.
chapters.es: Upon reaching the gates of Kiṣkindhā, Lakṣmaṇa fastens a gaja creeper around Sugrīva’s neck for identification. Rāma pledges to kill Vālin with a single arrow, citing his previous feat of piercing seven śāla trees. Encouraged, Sugrīva lets out a roar that scatters the forest deer and brings birds to the ground. This challenge echoes like crashing sea waves, summoning Vālin from the city to face his rival.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे पञ्चदशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Tārā advises Vālin against the duel.
chapters.es: Sugrīva’s roar reaches the inner apartments. Enraged, Vālin strides out with eyes like flaming fire. Tārā catches him in an embrace, pleading for caution. She warns that Sugrīva’s renewed confidence signals a powerful ally. Citing reports from Aṅgada, she identifies this protector as Rāma, a sheltering tree for the distressed. She urges Vālin to abandon the feud, crown his brother as yauvarājya, and seek peace.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे षोडशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma shoots Vālin during the duel.
chapters.es: Vālin rejects Tārā’s warnings and marches from the city. He finds Sugrīva waiting. The brothers bind their garments and exchange blows with clenched fists. Sugrīva uproots a śāla tree to strike Vālin, who staggers. As Sugrīva’s strength fails, Rāma releases an arrow resembling a venomous snake. The shaft pierces Vālin’s chest, and he falls to the earth like a toppled indradhvaja banner.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे सप्तदशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Vālin questions Rāma’s concealed strike.
chapters.es: Vālin collapses as Rāma’s arrow pierces his chest. Adorned with Indra’s golden mālā, the monkey king lies on the earth like a fallen celestial banner. As Rāma approaches, the wounded Vālin denounces the prince for striking from concealment. He challenges the ethics of a kṣatriya who kills a forest-dweller while hidden. Vālin asserts he could have retrieved Sītā himself, then falls silent as the pain overpowers him.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे अष्टादशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Rāma justifies the execution of Vālin.
chapters.es: Rāma justifies his actions to Vālin, explaining that the Ikṣvāku kings govern the earth to enforce dharma. He cites Vālin’s seizure of his brother’s wife as a transgression of smṛti requiring the death penalty. Comparing the monkey to forest game, Rāma defends his use of a concealed arrow. Vālin accepts these legal arguments and seeks protection for his son Aṅgada. Purged of sins through punishment, the monkey king asks for Rāma’s forgiveness.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे एकोनविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Tārā mourns over the dying Vālin.
chapters.es: Vālin lies dying on the forest floor. His wife Tārā rushes from the mountain caves and meets her panicked guards fleeing the battlefield. The monkeys urge her to secure the city and crown Aṅgada, but she rejects the kingdom to reach her husband's side. Finding Vālin fallen, she collapses in grief. Her cries move Sugrīva to remorse as he watches the queen and the young prince mourning their loss.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे विंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Tārā resolves to fast after Vālin’s death.
chapters.es: Tārā finds Vālin on the ground, pierced by Rāma’s arrow. She embraces his body, comparing the fallen king to an uprooted tree. Lamenting his silence, she claims he now favors the earth over her. She calls for their son, Aṅgada, to look upon his father one last time and asks Vālin to speak a final word. As other monkey women join the mourning, Tārā sits by her husband's side, intending to fast until death.

chapters.name: किष्किन्धाकाण्डे एकविंशः सर्गः
chapters.subtitle: Hanumān consoles the grieving Tārā.
chapters.es: Hanumān approaches Tārā as she falls in grief beside Vālin’s body. He describes the human frame as a fragile bubble and speaks of the inescapable fruits of action.
